progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: B9, B8, B7 and B5b: dominant, recessive, homozygous, heterozygous, carrier, autosome, the 2 x 2 square, ratios as chances per offspring, pedigree symbols and the giveaways (B9); the white-eyed male fly that appeared by mutation in 1910 (B8); genes code for enzymes and the white snapdragon with a non-working pigment enzyme (B7); each gamete gets one of each pair (B5b). Not assumed: genes on sex chromosomes, X-linked notation, incomplete dominance, co-dominance, multiple alleles, antigens.
progression.startsWith: Morgan's white-eyed flies that were all male, with the question of why eye colour should care whether a fly is male or female and why not every cross gives 3 to 1.
progression.stopsAfter: Saying a gene on the X has no partner on the Y so one recessive allele shows in a male; building X-linked crosses and reading sons and daughters separately; recognising the X-linked recessive pedigree pattern and ruling it out with an affected daughter of an unaffected father; reading the heterozygote first to tell complete, incomplete and co-dominance apart; explaining ABO as three alleles with two per person and predicting ABO crosses. No X-linked dominance, no Y-linked traits, no Rh factor, no conditional probability.
progression.nextLesson: G02: unfamiliar crosses and pedigrees with competing modes; then B11: frequencies of characteristics in a population.

teaching.task: Explain why some crosses do not give 3 to 1, and tell sex linkage, incomplete dominance, co-dominance and multiple alleles apart.
teaching.causalExplanation: A gene on the X has no partner on the Y, so a male with one recessive allele has nothing to hide it and shows it, while a female needs two. A father gives his X to every daughter and his Y to every son, so sons depend on the mother, a father never passes an X-linked allele to a son, and all his daughters are carriers. That is why X-linked recessive conditions are far more common in males and why an affected daughter of an unaffected father rules the pattern out. For other relationships, read the heterozygote first. One working enzyme copy makes less pigment, so a snapdragon heterozygote is pink, and the alleles do not blend because red and white return. In roan cattle each hair is fully red or fully white, so both alleles are expressed. Two heterozygotes give 1 : 2 : 1 in both because the heterozygote looks different from both homozygotes. The ABO gene has three alleles in the population but each person carries two, A and B are co-dominant, and the i enzyme does not work, so type O is only two i alleles and an A parent and a B parent who each carry i can have any group.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Opens on the white-eyed flies that were all male, builds the sex chromosomes and Morgan's cross on a square with daughter and son bands, applies it to haemophilia and the pedigree pattern, then asks why not every cross gives 3 to 1 and teaches incomplete dominance, co-dominance and ABO by reading the heterozygote first, gives the memory aids, then asks two harder unseen items with a short pause and brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Morgan's F2 flies gave white eyes again, but every white-eyed fly was male. Why would eye colour care whether a fly is male or female, and why do not all crosses give 3 to 1?
teaching.understandingCheck: Red-green colour blindness is an X-linked recessive allele: a woman with normal vision whose father was colour-blind has children with a man with normal vision, so find the chance of a colour-blind son among all children and among sons, and say whether a daughter could be colour-blind. Then a type A mother and a type B father have a type O child: give the genotypes and the chance that the next child is type AB.
teaching.curriculumScope: Model the formation of new combinations of genotypes produced during meiosis, including interpreting examples of sex-linkage, co-dominance, incomplete dominance and multiple alleles, and construct and interpret information from pedigrees and Punnett squares (Module 5, B5-IQ4-02, ACSBL085). X-linked dominance, Y-linked traits, Rh factor, epistasis and conditional probability are deferred.

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer, painted red and white-eyed flies, snapdragons, roan cattle and red blood cells, and coded X and Y chips with allele tags, daughter and son bands on the Punnett grid, a heterozygote board of rows, hair and petal zoom circles, antigen marks on a cell, a data-driven pedigree and a genotype table. Genotypes use superscripts on screen, never colour only. No people are drawn.
design.transitionPlan: The B8 jar and fly plates open the lesson and give way to the sex chromosome panels and the cross board for scenes 2 to 5; the heterozygote board builds one row per relationship from scene 6 to scene 9 and the cross board returns for the ABO square; each attempt card clears the board and its feedback shrinks the card to a strip and builds the model answer one point at a time; the next chip slides in; scene crossfade with settle.
